results.translation:
ON THE HISTORY OF PLANTS, notable commentaries, worked out with the greatest expense and vigils, to which are added more than five hundred living images of the same, never before produced and expressed with such artistic imitation of nature, by Leonhart Fuchs, physician by far the most distinguished of our age, as author.

Many, at great expense and with unwearied study, and sometimes not without danger to life, have visited foreign regions in order to procure for themselves the means of learning about materials of simple medicines: this whole subject-matter you will here be permitted to learn, with the greatest saving both of expense and of time, without any danger at all, as though in a living and most pleasant garden, with great delight.

There has also been added a quite concise explanation of the difficult and obscure terms occurring throughout this work.

Together with a fourfold Index, of which the first indeed contains the Greek names of the plants, the second the Latin, the third those in use among apothecaries' shops and herbalists, and the fourth will contain the German names.

[Woodcut of a tree/printer's device, labeled] PALMA ISING[RINI, the printer's mark]

It has moreover been provided for by decree of the most invincible Emperor Charles, that no one else may anywhere print these commentaries on the history of plants with impunity, according to the terms of the privilege previously published by us.

AT BASEL, IN THE PRINTING HOUSE OF ISINGRIN, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 1542.

A decoction heals by the fumigation of its vapor; or if it discharges matter, ground with honey. Three or four sprigs, with a single root of Gallic nard, drunk in six cyathi of water, provoke urine and menses. Taken privately with honey, and applied in a fleece [wool], it helps menses. It relieves quinsy [sore throat] when taken with honey and niter. It heals night-blisters (epinyctides) with water; and heals recent wounds if applied before they are touched by water; and likewise sores of the head. It is particularly applied to the flanks, mixed with Cyprian wax, or with fig. It also heals itching. It should not be given in fever. Drunk, it prevents seasickness during voyages; applied to the belly, it reduces swelling of the groin. Its smell induces sleep, or when placed under the head of one unaware. Inserted among clothes, it wards off moths. Mixed with oil, it drives away gnats when the anointed are smeared with it, and likewise when burned as smoke. Diluted in its preparation, it protects a scribe's ink [i.e., writing] from mice. The ash of wormwood, mixed with rose ointment, blackens the hair. The sea-wormwood, which some call seriphium, is harmful to the stomach. It softens the bowels, and expels the creatures of the intestines. It is drunk with oil and salt, or diluted in a gruel of three-month wheat flour. It is boiled, as much as a handful, in a sextarius of water down to half.

THE VIRTUES OF WORMWOOD WINE.
ACCORDING TO DIOSCORIDES.

Wormwood wine is suited to the stomach and provokes urine. It is useful for those who digest slowly; likewise for those with liver ailments, kidney troubles, and those afflicted by jaundice. It helps those who have no appetite for food, those with a poorly affected stomach, and those with long-standing distensions and bloating of the precordia, as well as round worms and suppressed menses. Drunk in greater quantity against the poison of mistletoe [ixia], and given after vomiting, it is beneficial.

PREPARATION.

There are various preparations of wormwood wine, as can be established from Dioscorides. However, the best is made if eight drachms of pounded Pontic wormwood, tied loosely in a linen cloth, are placed into an amphora of wine. Then the must is added, leaving one vent-hole of the vessel open so that the fermenting wine does not burst forth.

Santonicum, as has been mentioned, is today called 'seed of worms' [semen lumbricorum], and its principal use at this time is for expelling and killing worms from the body. And if it is genuine, it is taken with great efficacy mixed with honey, both by children and by adults. C ...interspersed with markings, so that it seems plainly to imitate the appearance and color of a serpent. At the leafy crown, six or seven leaves come forth, hanging down on a rather thick stalk about the length of fingers, sprinkled with reddish-purple spots, in the shape of the first kind of Dock (Rumex). From the leafy top of the stalk, a certain greenish sheath projects outward, gradually narrowing to a point like a spindle, as if it were the wrapping of an about-to-burst birth; when this splits open and spreads itself, it displays a purple horn tapering to a point. As the seed grows, [the sheath], stretched, bursts open into a crack, and finally, growing weak, becomes limp, and, drying up, perishes, leaving the horn behind. Around its lower part a clustered fruit surrounds it, with berries at first green, then glowing with a saffron and crimson color. The root, finally, is large, round, white, and clothed with a thin bark. And in sum, there is absolutely no feature that seems to contradict [this description].

HABITAT.
It grows in shady hedgerows.

SEASON.
The seed is gathered when it blackens with ripeness. The root is dug up at harvest time, that is, in the month of July or at the beginning of August.

TEMPERAMENT.
Dragon-wort (Dracunculus) is sharp and bitter, and has a certain slight astringency, so that no one can doubt it to be hot and dry.

VIRTUES, ACCORDING TO DIOSCORIDES.
The root has the power of warming. Roasted and boiled, licked up with honey, it is beneficial for those with difficulty breathing (orthopnoics), for ruptures, convulsions, coughs, and catarrhs. Drunk with wine it stimulates desire for intercourse. Cut up and applied with honey, it cleanses malignant and gangrenous ulcers, especially when combined with white bryony. From it and honey eye-salves are compounded for fistulas, and for inducing the expulsion of dead fetuses. It is effectively smeared with honey on vitiligo. It removes polyps and carcinomas.
D Its juice is useful for eye medicines, likewise against films, white spots, and dimness of the eyes. The smell of the herb and root spoils recently conceived pregnancies, causing miscarriage. Thirty grains of it taken in vinegar-water (posca) produce the same effect. Some pour its juice mixed with oil into the ears for earache. Its leaves too, being astringent, have been applied to fresh wounds, and, cooked in wine, to chilblains. It is said that those who rub the leaves on their hands, or carry the root, are not struck by a viper.

ACCORDING TO GALEN.
Dracontium has something very similar to Arum, both in its leaves and its root. It too is sharp and bitter, and of fine parts. It also possesses a certain mild astringency, which, since it is joined with the two aforementioned qualities—namely the sharp and the bitter—makes it a medicine that is, as it were, most effective. For the root purges all the internal organs, and especially thins thick and viscous humors. It is an excellent remedy for stubborn ulcers. It purges and cleanses vigorously both other conditions requiring abrasion, and also leprous spots (alphos) with vinegar. The leaves too, having a similar property, are suitable for ulcers and freshly inflicted wounds, and the less dry they are, the more they cause adhesion: for those that are drier have stronger powers than to be suitable for wounds. It is believed that if moist cheese is wrapped and stored covered with these [leaves], it is preserved from putrefaction because of their dry temperament. The fruit is more potent, not only the leaves but also the root: hence it is believed to dissolve cancers and polyps. Its juice also purges defects of the eyes. We sometimes administer the root of Dracontium, boiled twice or thrice to strip away all its medicinal potency, as food in the manner of Arum, when thick and glutinous humors afflicting the chest and lungs need to be expelled with greater force.

ACCORDING TO PLINY.
Serpents entirely flee one who has Dragon-wort. Therefore they say it is beneficial as a drink for those who have been struck [by a snake]; and it is said to stop menstruation, if it is not touched by iron. Its juice is also good for earache. ON ECHIUM. CHAPTER 102.

NAMES.
It is called Exion, or alkibiadion by the Greeks, Echion and Alcibiacum by the Latins. Unknown to pharmacists. Common herbalists call it wild Buglossum, following whom the Germans call it 'wild Ochsenzungen' (wild ox-tongue). Some hold that it is called Echion because it is useful against the bites of wild beasts. Others say it is because it flowers with little heads similar to a viper's. Dioscorides more correctly states it is so named because its seeds resemble a viper's head.

FORM.
It has leaves that are oblong, rough, thin, close to those of Anchusa (alkanet), yet smaller and fleshier. It also has slender prickles adjoining the leaves. It has many thin little stalks, and on both sides thin, feathered, black little leaflets, smaller in proportion toward the top of the stalk. Near the leaves are purple flowers, in which the seed is similar to a viper's head. The root is more slender than a finger, and somewhat blackish. From this description it becomes clearer than sunlight that the herb whose picture we present here is Echium. For it has very long, hairy, thin leaves, resembling those of Anchusa, yet smaller and fleshier, roughened with fine thorns; thin, numerous little stalks; and small leaves hanging down on both sides, black, becoming tiny at the top of the stem, among which purple flowers gleam, in which sit seeds resembling the little heads of vipers, tapering gradually from the neck into a small beak, with the upper part somewhat swollen, in which certain small protrusions appear like the sockets of eyes — something which I myself have observed with these very eyes not once, but again and again. The root, thinner than a finger, is blackish.

PLACE.
It grows almost everywhere along roadsides and in rough places.

TIME.
It flowers in the month of June.

TEMPERAMENT.
It is inferred to be warm, though not markedly dry, from the fact that it has the property of generating milk. For medicines that convert phlegmatic humors into blood by heating them are, as Galen testifies in Book Five, Chapter Twenty of 'On the Faculties of Simple Medicines,' wont to generate milk.

POWERS. FROM DIOSCORIDES.
The root, drunk with wine, not only helps those bitten by serpents, but also protects those who take it beforehand from being struck. The leaves and seed produce the same effect. It also soothes pains of the loins, and when taken with wine or as a broth, it stimulates milk.

FROM PAULUS.
Echium is a thorny herb which, drunk with wine, not only aids those bitten by a serpent, but also prevents those who take it beforehand from being struck.
